subjective.question: Define analytical chemistry.
subjective.answer: Differentiate between qualitative and quantitative analysis. Analytical chemistry is the branch of science that deals with the study and development of testing methods for determining the composition of substances. It has two main branches: (i) Qualitative analysis — it identifies what chemical species (elements, ions or compounds) are present in a sample. (ii) Quantitative analysis — it determines how much of a particular species (the analyte) is present in the sample. Analytical chemistry is applied in drug and food analysis laboratories, clinical chemistry, environmental monitoring and quality control of industrial products.

subjective.question: Define analyte and matrix. What are matrix effects and why are they important in an analysis?
subjective.answer: The analyte is the component or chemical species in a sample that is of interest in an analytical procedure, i.e. the substance whose identity or amount is to be determined. The matrix is everything else in the sample, i.e. all the components of the sample other than the analyte of interest. Matrix effects are the influences of the matrix on the way an analysis is conducted and on the quality of the results obtained. The matrix may enhance or suppress the analytical signal, interfere with the measurement, or change the behaviour of the analyte, so it must be considered while selecting and validating an analytical method.

subjective.question: What is sampling?
subjective.answer: Explain grab, composite and replicate samples. Sampling is the process of selecting a small portion of material (the sample) from a large bulk so that the sample truly represents the whole material. Important types of samples are: (i) Grab sample — a single sample collected at one place and one time; it represents the material only at that moment. (ii) Composite sample — a sample prepared by mixing a number of grab samples collected at different points or times; it gives an average picture and is preferred when a lot of variability is found in the material. (iii) Replicate samples — samples of the same size that are analyzed under similar analytical conditions; they are used to judge the precision of a method. (iv) Random sample — a sample selected without any bias so that every part of the bulk has an equal chance of being selected.

subjective.question: Why must a suspended analyte be coagulated before separation?
subjective.answer: Describe filtration as a separation technique. Coagulation is the process in which fine suspended particles join together to form larger aggregates (flocs). A suspended analyte is first coagulated because very fine suspended particles pass through ordinary filter media and cannot be separated directly; once they are coagulated into bigger particles, they can be separated easily by filtration or settling. Filtration is a very basic analytical technique used to separate solid insoluble particles from a liquid. The mixture is passed through a porous medium (filter paper or membrane); the liquid passes through as the filtrate while the insoluble solid is retained on the filter as the residue.

subjective.question: Describe the common sample preparation methods used before an instrumental analysis.
subjective.answer: Sample preparation converts the sample into a form suitable for measurement. Common methods are: (i) Dry ashing — the sample is heated strongly in a muffle furnace so that the organic matter is burnt off and the inorganic residue (ash) is left, which is then dissolved in acid. (ii) Wet digestion — the sample is decomposed by heating with strong acids (or acid mixtures) until a clear solution is obtained. (iii) Dilution — the sample is diluted with a suitable solvent to bring the analyte concentration within the working range of the instrument. (iv) Extraction — the analyte is transferred into a suitable solvent by solvent extraction or solid phase extraction. Instrumental calibration is not a sample preparation method; it is the adjustment/standardization of an instrument against known standards.

subjective.question: Compare solvent extraction and solid phase extraction as separation techniques.
subjective.answer: Solvent extraction is a separation technique that uses two immiscible liquids to separate a liquid or solid sample. The analyte distributes itself between the two liquid phases according to its solubility, and the phase containing the analyte is separated. The layer position depends on density: for example, chloroform (density greater than water) forms the bottom layer, while water forms the upper layer. In solid phase extraction, the liquid sample is passed through a solid adsorbent packed in a cartridge. The analyte is retained on the solid phase and is later recovered (eluted) with a small volume of a suitable solvent. It is used to separate and concentrate a soluble analyte from a liquid sample and needs much less solvent than liquid–liquid extraction.

subjective.question: Differentiate between determinate (systematic) and indeterminate (random) errors.
subjective.answer: Determinate (systematic) errors are errors that can be determined exactly and can be estimated; they have a known cause and a fixed direction, so they can be corrected or eliminated. They arise from instruments (instrumental errors, removed by calibration of equipment), methods, and personal faults of the analyst. Indeterminate (random) errors cannot be determined exactly; they arise from unknown and uncontrollable variations in measurements. They cause results to scatter around the mean value and can be minimized by careful work and repeated measurements, but they can never be eliminated completely. They are treated statistically, e.g. by standard deviation.

subjective.question: Differentiate between accuracy and precision with the help of the dart-board example.
subjective.answer: Accuracy is the closeness of a measured value to the true (actual) value; data completely free of error is accurate. Precision is the closeness of repeated measurements to each other, i.e. the reproducibility of results having the least variation among themselves. Precision is measured by the standard deviation. Dart-board example: if all darts hit close to the centre (bull's eye), the result is both accurate and precise. If the darts are tightly clustered away from the centre, the result is precise but not accurate. If the darts are scattered around the centre, the average may be accurate but the result is not precise. Maximum points are scored by targeting the mid circle of the board.

subjective.question: Define absolute error and relative error.
subjective.answer: A pipette, instead of giving an accurate measurement of 10 mL, gives 9.5 mL. Calculate its relative error. Absolute error is the difference between the measured value and the true value: E = measured value − true value. Relative error is the absolute error expressed relative to the true value, usually as a percentage: Relative error = (absolute error / true value) × 100. Calculation: true volume = 10 mL, measured volume = 9.5 mL. Absolute error = 9.5 − 10 = −0.5 mL. Relative error = (0.5 / 10) × 100 = 5%. Hence the relative error of the pipette is 5%.

subjective.question: For the readings 3, 7, 8, 5 and 10, calculate the mean and the median, and state the mode.
subjective.answer: Mean = sum of readings / number of readings = (3 + 7 + 8 + 5 + 10) / 5 = 33 / 5 = 6.6. Median is the middle value after arranging the data in ascending (or descending) order: 3, 5, 7, 8, 10. The middle (3rd) value is 7, so the median is 7. Mode is the most frequently occurring value. Every value occurs only once, so this data set has no mode.

subjective.question: Define variance, standard deviation and relative standard deviation.
subjective.answer: Calculate the variance and standard deviation of the readings 3, 7, 8, 5 and 10. Variance is the average of the squared deviations of the readings from their mean; it represents the spread (expand) of analytical data. For a sample, variance s² = Σ(xi − mean)² / (n − 1). Standard deviation (s) is the square root of the variance; it is the most common measure of precision. Relative standard deviation (RSD) is a special form of standard deviation, expressed relative to the mean: RSD = (s / mean) × 100 (in %) or × 1000 (in parts per thousand). RSD is always positive. Calculation for 3, 7, 8, 5, 10: mean = 6.6. Deviations: −3.6, 0.4, 1.4, −1.6, 3.4. Squared deviations: 12.96 + 0.16 + 1.96 + 2.56 + 11.56 = 29.20. Variance = 29.20 / (5 − 1) = 7.30. Standard deviation s = √7.30 ≈ 2.70. RSD = (2.70 / 6.6) × 100 ≈ 40.9%.

subjective.question: State the rules for rounding off numbers in analytical data.
subjective.answer: While rounding off a number to the required number of figures, the following rules are applied: (i) If the digit to be dropped is less than 5, the last retained digit is kept unchanged (retained). For example, 5.04 rounds to 5.0. (ii) If the digit to be dropped is greater than 5, the last retained digit is increased by 1. For example, 5.06 rounds to 5.1. (iii) If the digit to be dropped is exactly 5, the number is rounded so that the result ends with an even number. For example, 4.45 becomes 4.4 (the retained digit 4 is already even) and 4.35 becomes 4.4 (the retained digit is increased to make it even). Only one figure is dropped at a time, and rounding is done only at the final step of a calculation.

subjective.question: State Beer–Lambert law, give its mathematical form and define each term.
subjective.answer: Beer–Lambert law states that when a beam of light of a particular wavelength passes through a sample, its intensity decreases exponentially with the concentration of the absorbing species and the path length of the sample. In mathematical form: A=εlc where A = absorbance (log of incident intensity/transmitted intensity), ε = molar absorptivity (a constant for the analyte at the given wavelength), l = path length of the cell (usually in cm) and c = concentration of the analyte. Thus absorbance is directly proportional to concentration, which is the basis of quantitative estimation of unknowns by UV spectroscopy. All spectroscopic techniques that use electromagnetic radiation for quantitative work are based on this law.

subjective.question: A solution shows an absorbance of 0.450 in a 1 cm cell. If the molar absorptivity of the analyte is 1.5 × 10⁴ L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, calculate the concentration of the solution.
subjective.answer: From Beer–Lambert law: A = ε l c. Given A = 0.450, ε = 1.5 × 10⁴ L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, l = 1 cm. c = A / (ε l) = 0.450 / (1.5 × 10⁴ × 1) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L. Hence the concentration of the solution is 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L.

subjective.question: What is flame photometry?
subjective.answer: Give the flame colors of lithium, sodium, potassium and barium. Flame photometry is an emission technique in which the sample solution is sprayed into a flame; the heat of the flame excites the metal atoms, and the light emitted at a characteristic wavelength is measured to determine the concentration of the metal. Characteristic flame colors of some elements are: Lithium — red Sodium — yellow (golden yellow) Potassium — violet (lilac) Barium — lime green These colors help in the identification of the elements and form the basis of their quantitative estimation by flame photometry.

subjective.question: How is the concentration of an unknown sample estimated by UV spectroscopy?
subjective.answer: UV spectroscopy is one of the most common analytical techniques used in drug and food analysis laboratories and is commonly used to estimate the concentration of an unknown in a sample. The procedure is: (i) Prepare a series of standard solutions of known concentrations of the analyte. (ii) Measure the absorbance of each standard at the selected wavelength and plot a calibration curve of absorbance versus concentration; by Beer–Lambert law it is a straight line. (iii) Measure the absorbance of the unknown sample under the same conditions. (iv) Read the concentration of the unknown from the calibration curve (or calculate it from A = ε l c). Spectroscopy is the study of light and its interaction with matter; spectroscopic techniques use a particular type of electromagnetic radiation.

subjective.question: Calculate the mass of NaCl required to prepare 250 mL of 0.100 M NaCl solution.
subjective.answer: (Molar mass of NaCl = 58.44 g/mol) Mass of solute = molarity × volume (in litres) × molar mass. Molar mass of NaCl = 23 + 35.44 = 58.44 g/mol. Moles required = 0.100 mol/L × 0.250 L = 0.0250 mol. Mass = 0.0250 × 58.44 = 1.461 g. Hence 1.461 g of NaCl is weighed, dissolved in distilled water and the volume is made up to 250 mL in a volumetric flask.

subjective.question: List the seven basic quality control tools and explain any three of them.
subjective.answer: The seven basic quality control tools used to examine a data set are: (1) Cause and effect (fishbone/Ishikawa) diagram, (2) Check sheet, (3) Control chart, (4) Histogram, (5) Pareto diagram, (6) Scatter diagram and (7) Stratification. (i) Fishbone diagram — it is a quality control tool used to identify the root cause that is responsible for an effect; it presents a systematic representation of the relationship between the effect and the effecting factors. (ii) Pareto diagram — it is made by the combination of bar and line graphs of accumulated data and works on the principle of separating the "vital few" from the "trivial many". (iii) Histogram — the range of data is divided into smaller sections having a uniform span, and the number of occurrences is counted to develop a frequency distribution table; it helps to identify the location of the mean value.

subjective.question: What is a control chart? State the rule of seven consecutive points. What is a check sheet used for?
subjective.answer: A control chart is a quality control chart in which measured values are plotted against time or sample number together with the mean line and control limits; it shows whether a process is under statistical control. Rule of seven: if seven consecutive points (dots) fall below or above the mean value in a control chart, it indicates a problem in the process, even if all the points are within the control limits. The process should be examined and the cause removed. A check sheet is a simple form used to collect and record data in an organized way; it is used to perform stratification, i.e. to separate the data into categories so that patterns become visible.

subjective.question: Explain the method validation terms: linearity, range, robustness, LOD and LOQ.
subjective.answer: Linearity — the ability of a procedure to produce results that are directly proportional to the concentration of the analyte in the samples. Range — the interval between the lowest and highest levels of analyte that have been demonstrated to be determinable for the product, i.e. an expression of the lowest and highest levels shown to be measurable with acceptable accuracy and precision. Robustness — the ability of the procedure to provide analytical results of acceptable accuracy and precision under a variety of (deliberately changed) conditions; it shows the reliability of the method during normal use. Limit of Detection (LOD) — the smallest quantity of an analyte that can be detected, though not necessarily determined in a quantitative fashion. Limit of Quantitation (LOQ) — the lowest quantity of an analyte that can be determined quantitatively with acceptable accuracy and precision.

subjective.question: What is ISO? Differentiate between accreditation and certification. What does BMR stand for?
subjective.answer: ISO (International Organization for Standardization) creates documents that provide requirements, specifications, guidelines or characteristics that can be used consistently to ensure that materials, products, processes and services are fit for their purpose. Accreditation is a process of validation set by a peer review board, in which an authoritative body formally recognizes that a laboratory or organization is competent to carry out specific tasks. Certification is the written assurance by a third party that a product, process or system conforms to the specified requirements. Quality itself is a blend of design and manufacturing characteristics of a product to meet the customer's requirements. In pharmaceutical production, the complete record of a batch is maintained as the BMR — Batch Manufacturing Records.
